job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my laptop by eight-thirty in a shared office in Westlands, Nairobi. I'm a junior developer at a small fintech that helps shops take mobile payments. My day is mostly fixing bugs, building small features, and arguing politely in code review. I have an AI assistant in my editor from morning to evening, and I talk to it more than to some of my colleagues. Evenings I'm either at a coding meetup or at my mother's pharmacy doing the stock count.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me how you ended up there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did software engineering at Strathmore and finished with a good result. For my final project I built a stock tracking app for small pharmacies, which is how I ended up with my mother's shop as my first client. I did a three-month internship at a bank's IT department. The fintech hired me in July. I share a flat with my friend Wanjiru, I owe about nine thousand in loans and fees, and I have about six weeks of costs saved. My dad is a retired teacher and he'd help if I really needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's possible. I use these tools all day and they're helpful, but they get plenty of things wrong and you need to know the code to catch it. At work I'd say let's use them for the boring bits and keep humans for the design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit uneasy, and not about AI. My company is small and depends on a few big shop chains. If one of them leaves, there's not much runway. A startup can disappear in a quarter, and I'm the newest developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and improving, and I'd build the pharmacy app a bit more, since there are about forty other small pharmacies I could sell it to. I'd save about ten percent of my pay and try to reach three months of costs. And I'd start going to the meetup talks about backend systems, which is what I'd like to be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, sort of excited. I like building, and a world where nothing breaks my career is a good world for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the fintech folds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a month or two of savings, a decent CV and a pharmacy app. I'd move quickly to apply to banks, because they hire juniors and they're steady. It would be a shock, but I've seen friends do it, and they were okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start with pharmacies and not bigger businesses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know them. My mother tells me what annoys her, and I'm not guessing. A big firm has a hundred people deciding, but a pharmacy owner can say yes in a phone call.

say: The tools are **helpful but wrong** often, so you need to know the code.
Use them for boring bits and keep **humans** for design.
think: My company is small and depends on **a few shop chains**.
A startup can disappear in a **quarter**, and I'm the newest developer.
do: Build the **pharmacy app** and sell it to some of the forty pharmacies nearby.
Save **ten percent** of pay and reach three months of costs.
Go to **backend** talks at the meetup.
S0.quote: A startup can disappear in a quarter, and I'm the newest developer.
fieldNote: Her unease is about the **startup**, not AI.
She builds a second income from a **real customer**, her mother's pharmacy.
Daily AI user who judges tools by their errors.

steps.text: Sell the pharmacy stock app to five more local pharmacies
Save ten percent of every pay cheque
Keep fixing bugs and building features at the fintech

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I see already and it's going to speed up. At work I'd say we should write tests and review the AI's code properly. Online I'd say people entering tech need to learn judgement, not just syntax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think juniors like me are the ones who feel it most. The simple tickets I get now, like small bug fixes, are what the assistant does in a minute. Our firm might decide it needs one senior who uses AI instead of three juniors. I might be the one cut, or the firm might simply not hire the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to take on more customer-facing work, since talking to shop owners is something the tools don't do. I'd ask for ownership of one small product area to show I'm more than tickets. I'd also pick up a cloud certificate and spend a weekend a month on the pharmacy app. And I'd keep my CV updated every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight, but I think I like that pressure. I'd be anxious if I wasn't learning. I'm anxious about the pay, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would owning a product area look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the refund flow, which is dull but important, and make it my thing. I'd write the docs, fix the weird cases and keep track of the numbers. If somebody asks who knows about refunds, they should say my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like the pressure. Is that true when pay is at stake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I like the pressure when I can see what to do. The pay worry is separate. If they cut my hours or pay, I'd feel it in my stomach. My loan doesn't care that I was being brave.

say: It's already happening and it will **speed up**.
People entering tech need to learn **judgement**, not just syntax.
think: Juniors feel it **most**, since small bug fixes are what the assistant does in a minute.
The firm could want **one senior** with AI instead of three juniors.
do: Take on more **customer-facing** work with shop owners.
Ask to **own** the refund flow as my product area.
Get a **cloud certificate** and keep the CV fresh.
feel: **Tight**, but I like the pressure when I can see what to do.
S1.quote: My loan doesn't care that I was being brave.
fieldNote: Adaptive, but she's honest that **brave talk** doesn't pay a loan.
Wants to **own** something, so her name is the one people say.
Distinguishes pressure she likes from pay pressure she doesn't.

steps.text: Ask to own the refund flow and write its docs
Finish a cloud certificate by March
Spend one weekend a month improving the pharmacy app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to treat it as an emergency, and not pretend we know what's coming. At work I'd tell my boss that if the firm wants to survive it should use the tools harder than anybody. Online I'd back anything that gives workers a floor, like cash support, because two years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Coding is the thing AI does best. By 2028 a small fintech like ours could run with two engineers or none, and a junior with a year of experience is the easiest to replace. Robots would take about three more years to reach hands-on work, so the safe trades come later, but I'm not a trades person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every shilling and cut out eating out, taxis and my meetup passes. I'd double down on the pharmacy app and try to sign thirty shops before the firm lets me go. I'd also move my stuff to my parents' house in Kileleshwa, and I'd ask my dad if I could use my brother's old room. And I'd apply to ten banks and telecoms, because large firms are slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heart in my throat. I'd feel sick, then busy. Busy is what saves me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think large firms are slower to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they have rules, committees, contracts and old systems that nobody wants to touch. A bank takes two years to approve a new font. That's not good for the world, but it might buy me some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother, who runs the pharmacy, that my job is in danger and that the app is my real plan. She'd offer to be my first reference customer and tell all her friends. She'd be proud and scared, and she wouldn't say which one.

say: Treat it as an **emergency** and don't pretend we know what's coming.
If the firm wants to survive it should use the tools **harder** than anybody.
think: Coding is what AI does best, and a small fintech could run with **two engineers or none**.
A junior with a year of experience is **easiest to replace**.
do: Save every shilling and cut **taxis and eating out**.
Try to sign **thirty shops** to the pharmacy app.
Apply to **ten banks and telecoms**, which change slowly.
feel: **Sick, then busy**, and busy is what saves me.
S2.quote: A bank takes two years to approve a new font. That's not good for the world, but it might buy me some time.
fieldNote: Coding is her **own** field, so the fear is specific and well informed.
Plans to run toward **large slow firms** for shelter.
Her mother would become the first reference customer.

steps.text: Cut taxis, eating out and the meetup passes
Put every spare shilling into an emergency account
Sign thirty pharmacies to the stock app before 2028
Apply to ten banks and telecoms for junior roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning that most people will waste. At work I'd say, let's invest in the people who know how to run the AI systems. Online I'd say schools and universities should start teaching this now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious, but I'd feel like I had a fighting chance. I'd be 27 in 2031. If I put in five good years, I could be the sort of engineer who runs AI systems or builds a business on top of them. I'd worry about whether there'd be a place for junior-to-mid developers in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these years to move from writing code to designing systems and talking to customers. I'd get the pharmacy app to a point where it earns about two hundred thousand shillings a month, which is maybe half my pay. I'd start putting money into a money market fund and a small plot of land my dad has a share in. And I'd probably leave the fintech for a bigger firm after two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and alive. A bit overwhelmed on a bad day, but I'd rather be in the middle of this than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing yet. Land doesn't care about AI. It's a safety net that I can't copy and paste. My dad's brother would let me build a small rental room there eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why leave the fintech for a bigger firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a bigger firm will still be here in 2031. A startup with five of us might not. Bigger firms also train juniors properly, and I'd want a name on my CV that people recognise.

say: Five years is a warning most people will **waste**.
Schools and universities should start teaching **this** now, not in year four.
think: I'd be anxious, but with a **fighting chance** as someone who runs AI systems.
I worry about the **junior-to-mid** developer gap.
do: Move from writing code to **designing systems** and customer work.
Grow the pharmacy app to earn **half my pay**.
Put money into a **money market fund** and family land.
feel: **Alert and alive**, and I'd rather be in the middle of this.
S3.quote: Land doesn't care about AI. It's a safety net that I can't copy and paste.
fieldNote: Takes a **portfolio** approach: skills, side income, and land.
Wants a **recognisable** employer for stability by 2031.
Prefers to be inside the change rather than outside.

steps.text: Grow the pharmacy app to earn about half my salary
Put money into a money market fund each month
Move to a bigger firm after two years at the fintech
Take on system design and customer calls at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the clever thing is to build something people want. At work I'd say let's plan careers for people who work with AI. Online I'd say kids should learn to ask better questions of these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd be 32, and with ten years I could do a master's, run my own company, or get senior at a large firm. The danger is getting lazy because the deadline feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the fintech for two years, then maybe go for a master's in machine learning, part-time. I'd grow the pharmacy app into a proper company with two employees. I'd also put money into shares each month and help my parents with a new roof. I'd say yes to speaking at meetups, which would grow my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised. I'd be in my best years, with time to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your first hire in the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person who sells, not a developer. I can write the code with the assistant, but I'm not good at calling a chemist and asking for a meeting. I'd look for someone like my friend Wanjiru, who can talk to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep from drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a calendar alert on the first of every month to write what I shipped and what I learned. Ten years turns into three months of nothing if I don't. Having a small public record helps.

say: Ten years is long, so build **something people want**.
Kids should learn to ask **better questions** of these systems.
think: With a decade I could do a **master's**, run a company or get senior.
The danger is getting **lazy** because the deadline feels far.
do: Do a part-time master's in **machine learning** after two years.
Grow the pharmacy app into a **company** with two employees.
Invest monthly in **shares** and help my parents repair their roof.
feel: **Energised**, in my best years with time to try things.
S4.quote: Ten years turns into three months of nothing if I don't. Having a small public record helps.
fieldNote: Her first hire would be a **seller**, an honest view of her own gap.
The monthly check is her answer to **drift**.
Plans include helping her parents with a **roof**.

steps.text: Start a part-time machine learning master's after two years
Turn the pharmacy app into a company with a sales hire
Put money into shares every month
Keep working at the fintech and building a public record of projects

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because coding is the first thing to go and I'm a coder. What would help is time and a place to learn the next skill for free, some cash support if jobs vanish quickly, and big firms that hire juniors even when AI could do the task.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that using AI every day doesn't make me a fan, and it doesn't make me a victim either. I'm just someone who sees it up close. I see where it's brilliant and where it's confidently wrong.

headlineQuote: Using AI every day doesn't make me a fan, and it doesn't make me a victim either.
portrait: Esther Farah is **22**, a junior developer at a small Nairobi fintech, sharing a flat with a friend.
She did software engineering, owes about **nine thousand** and has six weeks of costs saved.
She's a centrist and adaptive, uses **AI all day** and has her mother's pharmacy as her first app customer.
Her mood climbs to **alarmed** at AGI in two years, when she'd save hard, sell the app and apply to banks.
With time she plans systems work, a bigger employer, a **master's** and maybe her own company.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **coding** is the first thing to go.
whatWouldHelp: Time and free places to learn, **cash support** for fast job loss, and big firms that keep hiring juniors.
